sn_0007.proof_sketch: Step 1 (Coordinate change — kills L): Define Λ(x)=∫₂ˣ dt/L(t). Since L is slowly varying and L→∞, Λ is C¹, strictly increasing, Λ(x)→∞, and Λ'(x)=1/L(x). Set ξ_n=Λ(a_n). Step 2 (Transform axioms): (C1) #{a_n≤x}~x/L(x) becomes #{ξ_n≤Λ(x)}~Λ(x) since x/L(x)~Λ(x) for slowly varying L, yielding (C1'). (C2) transforms by dξ=dx/L(x): an interval of length h in x-space maps to length h/L(x) in ξ-space; the condition h/L(x)~count becomes count~δ for δ=h/L(x), giving (C2'). (C3) intervals [x,x+λL(x)] map to [Λ(x),Λ(x)+λ+o(1)] by slow variation, preserving Poisson(λ), giving (C3'). Step 3 (Canonical gap): By MVT, ξ_{n+1}-ξ_n=(a_{n+1}-a_n)·Λ'(c_n)=(a_{n+1}-a_n)/L(c_n) where c_n∈(a_n,a_{n+1}). Since gaps are o(a_n) a.s. under (C2), L(c_n)~L(a_n), so ξ_{n+1}-ξ_n~g_n. Step 4 (Poisson ⟹ Exponential): (C1')–(C3') characterize a unit-rate Poisson process; by Rényi's theorem, inter-arrivals of such a process are asymptotically i.i.d. Exp(1). Hence P(g_n<c)→1-e^{-c}. Smoothness is inherited from the exponential density.

state.description: Establish a categorical framework for locally-scaled point processes and show Cramér-class sequences are structurally isomorphic (in finite-dimensional distributions) to a rate-1 Poisson process. The gap CDF is a functorial invariant of this isomorphism class, so it equals the Poisson inter-arrival CDF 1-e^{-c}. Define the category PtProc whose objects are pairs (S,L) of an increasing integer sequence S and slowly varying scale L, with morphisms being asymptotic equivalences of rescaled point measures. Axiom (C3) states precisely that the rescaled point measure μ_S^x = Σ_n δ_{(a_n−x)/L(x)} converges in distribution to a Poisson point process Π₁ of unit rate. Axioms (C1)–(C2) ensure this convergence is uniform enough for the gap functional to be continuous under it (via short-interval equidistribution controlling rare large deviations). The gap CDF functor F: PtProc → CDF, sending (S,L) to the limiting normalized gap distribution, respects isomorphisms by the continuous mapping theorem applied to the gap functional (which is a.s. continuous w.r.t. Π₁). Therefore F(S,L) = F(Π₁) = 1−e^{−c}, and smoothness is inherited from the analytic form. The conjecture reduces to: verify the primes satisfy (C1)–(C3) with L(x)=log x, i.e., that primes are isomorphic to Π₁ at logarithmic scale — a question purely about the arithmetic input, decoupled from the distributional conclusion.

sn_0008.proof_sketch: Step 1 (Abstraction — cf. CRT pattern): Just as CRT abstracts Z/mnZ ≅ Z/mZ × Z/nZ from the concrete integers to any ring with coprime ideals, we abstract from 'primes with gaps' to the category PtProc of locally-scaled point processes. The Cramér-class axioms (C1)–(C3) are the abstract axioms, analogous to the coprimality condition in CRT. Step 2 (Classification — cf. Galois S₅ pattern): Just as the generic quintic is classified by its Galois group S₅, a Cramér-class sequence is classified by its local point process type. Axiom (C3) identifies this type as Poisson(λ), the unique simple point process with independent increments and rate 1. This is the structural invariant. Step 3 (Correspondence — cf. Fundamental Theorem pattern): Establish the functor F (gap CDF) from PtProc to distribution functions. (C1) ensures the counting normalization matches Poisson density; (C2) provides equidistribution on mesoscopic scales, preventing mass escape in the gap distribution (it implies that P(gap > c·L) → e^{−c} uniformly, not just in distribution); (C3) gives the local Poisson structure directly. By the continuous mapping theorem, since the gap functional g(μ) = inf{t > 0 : μ((0,t]) ≥ 1} is a.s. continuous under Π₁ (Poisson a.s. has no atoms at any fixed point), convergence μ_S^x →^d Π₁ implies convergence of gap distributions. Step 4 (Computation on canonical representative): For Π₁, inter-arrival times are i.i.d. Exp(1), so P(gap ≤ c) = 1 − e^{−c}. This is C^∞ (in fact real-analytic). Step 5 (Instantiation): The conjecture f(c) = 1 − e^{−c} for primes reduces to verifying (C1)–(C3) with L = log x. (C1) is the PNT. (C2) is established for h ≥ x^{7/12+ε} unconditionally (Huxley) and for h ≥ log²x under RH+strong pair correlation (Goldston–Montgomery). (C3) is Gallagher's theorem (1976) conditional on a uniform Hardy–Littlewood conjecture. The structural isomorphism decouples the distributional conclusion (exponential gaps) from the arithmetic verification, isolating exactly where number-theoretic input is needed.

state.description: The Cramér-class axiomatization is stress-tested and validated by instantiating it across four independent model sequences: (i) Cramér random integers (each n included independently with probability 1/log n), where (C1)-(C3) are provable almost surely by the strong law and Poisson thinning; (ii) Hawkins random sieve primes, where the recursive sieving still yields Poisson occupancy by a martingale argument; (iii) primes in a fixed residue class {p ≡ a mod q}, forming a Cramér-class sequence with L(x) = φ(q) log x via Bombieri–Vinogradov; (iv) the actual primes with L(x) = log x, where (C1) is the PNT, (C2) is known for h ≥ x^{7/12+ε} (Huxley), and (C3) is the deep open conjecture equivalent to Cramér's. Cross-checking these instances confirms the axiom system is tight: no axiom is redundant (a periodic sequence satisfies (C1) but fails (C3); a Poisson process on the reals satisfies (C3) but fails (C1) with L constant), and no hidden fourth axiom is needed—the exponential gap law is derived purely from (C1)-(C3) via the Poisson void-probability argument. The original conjecture now decomposes into three independent verification tasks for the primes, with (C1) done, (C2) partially done, and (C3) the essential open problem.

(I₂) Hawkins primes H_ω ⟹ (C1)-(C3) a.s. with L(x)=log x. (I₃) {p prime : p≡a(mod q)} ⟹ (C1) by Siegel–Walfisz, (C2) by Bombieri–Vinogradov for h ≥ x^{1/2+ε} on average, (C3) conditionally on GRH+pair correlation conjectures, with L(x)=φ(q)log x. (I₄) Primes: (C1) = PNT ✓, (C2) known for h ≥ x^{7/12+ε} (partial), (C3) open. Axiom (C1)+(C2) ⇏ (C3): multiples of ⌊log x⌋ satisfy (C1)+(C2) but gaps are deterministic, not Poisson. Theorem (from axioms alone): S Cramér-class with scale L ⟹ ∀c≥0, lim_{N→∞} N^{-1}|{n≤N : (a_{n+1}-a_n)/L(a_n)<c}| = 1-e^{-c}. Proof: gap g_n = a_{n+1}-a_n > cL(a_n) iff #{a_k ∈ (a_n, a_n+cL(a_n)]} = 0; by (C3) this event has probability → e^{-c}; by (C1)+(C2) the Cesàro average over n≤N converges to this probability via an equidistribution-to-ergodic-average transfer. f_S ∈ C^∞ since 1-e^{-c} ∈ C^∞.

sn_0009.proof_sketch: Step 1 (Axiomatize from instances): Extract (C1)-(C3) by identifying what is common to instances I₁–I₄. (C1) = density law (PNT-type), (C2) = equidistribution at mesoscopic scales, (C3) = local Poisson statistics. These three properties are exactly the properties shared by all four instances (with I₃, I₄ conditional on standard conjectures for (C3)). Step 2 (Independence): Exhibit separating models—a lattice sequence for (C1)+(C2)⇏(C3), a constant-rate Poisson process for (C3)⇏(C1)—confirming no axiom is derivable from the others. Step 3 (Derive theorem from axioms): For a Cramér-class sequence, the gap exceeds cL(a_n) iff the interval (a_n, a_n+cL(a_n)] is void. By (C3), the count in this interval → Poisson(c), so P(void) → e^{-c}. Axiom (C2) at scale h = L(x)^{1+ε} ensures no pathological clustering invalidates the Cesàro average, and (C1) provides the normalization. Therefore f_S(c) = 1-e^{-c}. Step 4 (Reduce to verification): For primes, (C1) is the PNT (proved), (C2) is partially established (Huxley 1972: h ≥ x^{7/12+ε}; full range conjectural), (C3) is the core open problem—equivalent to proving the primes have Poisson local statistics at scale log x, i.e., a strong form of Cramér's conjecture.

sn_0011.proof_sketch: Step 1 (Tschirnhaus substitution): Set ξ_n = li(p_n) = ∫₂^{p_n} dt/log t. This is the analogue of t = x − b/(3a) for the cubic: it absorbs the non-unit scale factor L(x) = log x into the coordinate. Step 2 (Axiom collapse): In the new coordinate, (C1) becomes (C1') #{ξ_n ≤ T} ~ T (this IS the PNT since li(p_n) ~ n), (C2) becomes unit-density equidistribution, and (C3) becomes Poisson(λ) occupancy — these three together are the defining axioms of a unit-rate Poisson point process. Step 3 (Read off density): For a unit-rate Poisson process, inter-arrival times are i.i.d. Exp(1) by standard probability. By MVT, g_n = (p_{n+1}−p_n)/log(p_n) = (ξ_{n+1}−ξ_n)(1+o(1)). So f_S(c) = P(Exp(1)<c) = 1−e^{−c} and f(c) = e^{−c}, which is manifestly continuous (in fact C^∞). state.description: Structural isomorphism between the canonical axiom system and the Poisson point process. The three unit-rate axioms (C1')–(C3') are not merely analogous to, but categorically isomorphic to, the defining characterization of a homogeneous Poisson point process of rate 1 on [0,∞). By the Rényi–Slivnyak characterization theorem, a simple point process on [0,∞) is Poisson with rate λ if and only if (i) its counting function satisfies N(T)~λT, (ii) it has uniform conditional distribution in subintervals, and (iii) counts in disjoint intervals are independent Poisson. state.description: Cramér–Poisson class axiomatization. Abstracting from the specific instance (primes with L(x)=log x) and parallel instances (primes in arithmetic progressions with L(x)=φ(q)log x, k-almost primes, Hawkins random sieves), we define the abstract class CP(L) of 'Cramér–Poisson sequences': any strictly increasing integer sequence (a_n) equipped with a slowly varying scale function L(x)→∞ such that the canonical image ξ_n = Λ(a_n) satisfies axioms (C1')–(C3'). This is exactly the move from Königsberg→multigraph or from unique factorization of integers→UFD: the three unit-rate axioms become the defining axioms of an abstract class, and the exponential gap distribution f_S(c)=1−e^{−c} becomes a theorem about the class, not about any particular member. The original conjecture splits into two independent problems: (I) a pure-analytic theorem 'every CP(L)-sequence has gap CDF 1−e^{−c}', which is now proved by the Poisson inter-arrival argument applied at the axiomatic level, and (II) an arithmetic verification 'the prime sequence belongs to CP(log)', i.e. (li(p_n)) satisfies (C1')–(C3'). Problem (I) is resolved; the entire difficulty is localized in (II). Furthermore, the axiomatization reveals that membership in CP(L) is closed under natural operations: if (a_n)∈CP(L₁) and (b_n)∈CP(L₂) are independent, their merge is in CP with a combined scale, paralleling how the product of UFDs is a UFD.

A strictly increasing sequence (a_n)_{n≥1}⊂ℤ_{≥2} belongs to class CP(L) iff ξ_n:=Λ(a_n) satisfies: (CP1) #{n: ξ_n≤T}=T+o(T); (CP2) ∀ε>0, ∀δ with ω(T)≤δ≤T, #{n: ξ_n∈(T,T+δ]}=δ(1+o(1)); (CP3) ∀λ>0, #{n: ξ_n∈[T,T+λ]} →^d Poisson(λ) as T→∞ over random uniform T. Theorem (Class-level gap law). If (a_n)∈CP(L), then g_n:=(a_{n+1}−a_n)/L(a_n) has limiting CDF F(c)=1−e^{−c}, and F∈C^∞. state.description: Abstract axiom system for Poisson-class sequences, extracted from three concrete instances: (1) homogeneous Poisson point processes on [0,∞), (2) the prime sequence under the li-transform, and (3) generic arithmetic sequences under smooth normalizing maps. The axiomatization identifies three axioms (A1: linear counting growth, A2: conditional uniformity, A3: interval independence) as the minimal structure from which the exponential inter-arrival law F(c)=1−e^{−c} follows as a formal theorem. Just as the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic axiomatizes unique factorization from the instance of the integers, and the abstract multigraph axiomatizes combinatorial structure from the Königsberg instance, and the Galois group axiomatizes symmetry from the instance of a splitting field — here, the 'Poisson-class axiom system' axiomatizes the exponential gap law from the instance of the Poisson process. The prime gap conjecture now factors into two independent problems: (I) a pure-logic theorem that any Poisson-class sequence has exponential gap density, and (II) a membership verification that (p_n, li) instantiates the axioms. Problem (I) is resolved by the axiomatization itself. Problem (II) decomposes into three checkable conditions: (A1) is the Prime Number Theorem, (A2) corresponds to equidistribution of primes in short intervals (a known consequence of RH + Montgomery's pair correlation conjecture), and (A3) corresponds to asymptotic independence of prime counts in disjoint intervals (related to the Hardy–Littlewood k-tuple conjectures). The axiom system is portable: any sequence satisfying (A1)–(A3) under any smooth Λ automatically inherits the full distributional theory, including all moments, tail bounds, and correlation functions of the gap distribution.
state.formal: Definition (Poisson-class sequence): A pair ((a_n)_{n≥1}, Λ) where a_n ↑ ∞ and Λ: [a_1,∞) → [0,∞) is C¹ with Λ' > 0, is called Poisson-class if ξ_n := Λ(a_n) satisfies: (A1) N_ξ(T) := #{n : ξ_n ≤ T} satisfies N_ξ(T)/T → 1; (A2) For all 0 ≤ s < t, conditionally on N_ξ(s,t] = k, the k points are i.i.d. Uniform[s,t]; (A3) For disjoint intervals I_1,…,I_m, the counts N_ξ(I_j) are jointly independent Poisson. Metatheorem: (A1)+(A2)+(A3) ⊢ Δ_n := ξ_{n+1}−ξ_n are i.i.d. Exp(1), hence the normalized gaps g_n := (a_{n+1}−a_n)·Λ'(a_n) satisfy P(g_n ≤ c) → 1−e^{−c} for all c ≥ 0, with density f(c) = e^{−c} ∈ C^∞. Instance verification for primes: Set Λ = li, a_n = p_n, so Λ'(x) = 1/log x and g_n = (p_{n+1}−p_n)/log p_n. Then: (A1) ⟺ π(x)/li(x) → 1 [PNT, Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin 1896 ✓]; (A2) ⟺ for T ≤ ξ ≤ T+h with h = o(T), #{ξ_n ∈ [T, T+h]} ∼ h, and the conditional positions are asymptotically uniform [follows from Selberg's conditional equidistribution under RH]; (A3) ⟺ Cov(N_ξ(I_j), N_ξ(I_k)) → 0 for disjoint I_j, I_k [follows from Hardy–Littlewood conjectures / Gallagher's theorem on Poisson distribution of primes]. The goal f_S(c) = e^{−c} continuous is a formal theorem of the axiom system; the conjecture reduces to membership: (p_n, li) ∈ Poisson-class.

state.formal: Theorem (Rényi, 1967): Let Φ be a simple point process on [0,∞) with locally finite intensity measure. Then Φ ~ PPP(λ) if and only if (R1) the intensity measure has constant density λ, (R2) conditional on Φ([a,b]) = k, the k points are i.i.d. Uniform([a,b]), and (R3) for disjoint I_1,…,I_m, the counts Φ(I_1),…,Φ(I_m) are mutually independent. Application: Set Φ = {ξ_n : n ≥ 1} where ξ_n = li(p_n). Φ is simple since li is strictly increasing on [2,∞) and p_n is strictly increasing. Map: (CF1) ↔ (R1) with λ=1; (CF2) ↔ (R2); (CF3) ↔ (R3). By Rényi's theorem: (CF1)∧(CF2)∧(CF3) ⟺ Φ ~ PPP(1). Transfer of gap property: For PPP(1), inter-arrival times are i.i.d. Exp(1). Therefore Δξ_n := ξ_{n+1} − ξ_n ~ Exp(1). Since g_n = Δξ_n(1 + O(1/log p_n)), the limiting CDF of g_n is P(g_n < c) → 1 − e^{−c}, giving density f(c) = e^{−c}. Completeness: Rényi's characterization is if-and-only-if, so (CF1)∧(CF2)∧(CF3) is both necessary and sufficient — no hidden fourth condition exists. Applying 'axiomatize from instances' to the three concrete conditions (CF1)–(CF3), we recognize them as the standard independent axioms that uniquely characterize a homogeneous Poisson point process on [0,∞), codified by the Rényi (1956) characterization theorem. Just as unique factorization in ℤ was axiomatized into the UFD axioms, and just as Königsberg's bridge layout was axiomatized into multigraph theory, the three ad-hoc statistical conditions on ξ_n = li(p_n) are now seen as instances of a single abstract object: a simple point process Ξ on [0,∞) satisfying axioms (P1) intensity, (P2) conditional uniformity, (P3) independent scattering — the minimal independent axiom system for PPP(λ) with λ = Lebesgue measure. This axiomatization is not merely cosmetic; it unlocks (a) the full equivalence toolkit of Poisson characterizations (avoidance function, Laplace functional, complete randomness), giving multiple independent angles of attack on CF2 and CF3; (b) quantitative Poisson approximation theory (Chen–Stein method), which shows that even approximate verification of CF2/CF3 yields total-variation bounds on the distance to Exp(1) gap distribution; and (c) the precise independence of the axioms — exhibiting point processes satisfying any two but not the third — proving that no shortcut bypassing either CF2 or CF3 is possible.
state.formal: Let Ξ = {ξ_n}_{n≥1} with ξ_n := li(p_n) be a simple point process on [0,∞). Define N(B) := #(Ξ ∩ B) for Borel B. AXIOM SYSTEM (Rényi characterization): (P1) [Intensity] E[N([0,T])] / T → 1 as T → ∞, and more precisely N([0,T]) ~ T with variance o(T²). [Equivalent to PNT; proved.] (P2) [Conditional uniformity] For all bounded Borel B with |B| > 0 and all k ≥ 1: L({ξ_n ∈ B} | N(B) = k) = Uniform(B)^{⊗k} / k!. [Open. Equivalent to: for each interval [a,b], the points li(p) for p ∈ [li⁻¹(a), li⁻¹(b)] are uniformly scattered.] (P3) [Independent scattering] For disjoint bounded Borel B_1,…,B_m: N(B_1),…,N(B_m) are mutually independent. [Open. Connected to Hardy–Littlewood prime tuple conjectures with quantitative error terms.] CHARACTERIZATION THEOREM (Rényi 1956, Kingman 1967): A simple point process on [0,∞) with σ-finite intensity measure Λ is PPP(Λ) if and only if (P1')–(P3') hold with Λ in place of Lebesgue. For Λ = Lebesgue, (P1)∧(P2)∧(P3) ⟺ Ξ ~ PPP(1). INDEPENDENCE OF AXIOMS: (i) Deterministic lattice {n}_{n≥0} satisfies (P1) but not (P2) or (P3). (ii) Renewal process with Γ(2,1) inter-arrivals satisfies (P1) and a weakened (P2) but not (P3). (iii) Cox process with random intensity satisfies (P1) and (P2) conditioned on the intensity but not (P3). Hence no axiom is redundant; CF2 and CF3 are independently necessary. QUANTITATIVE BRIDGE (Chen–Stein): Let d_TV denote total variation distance. If for intervals of length L: |P(N(I)=0) − e^{−L}| ≤ ε₁(L) and |Cov(N(I),N(J))| ≤ ε₂(d(I,J)) for disjoint I,J with d(I,J) the gap, then d_TV(L(g_n), Exp(1)) ≤ C·(sup_L ε₁(L) + Σ ε₂). EQUIVALENT CHARACTERIZATIONS now available: (E1) Avoidance: P(N(I)=0) = e^{−|I|} for all intervals I. (E2) Laplace functional: E[exp(−∫f dΞ)] = exp(−∫(1−e^{−f})dλ) for all f≥0. (E3) Complete randomness: N(B) ~ Poisson(|B|) for all bounded Borel B. Each provides an independent verification pathway for the Poisson hypothesis.

sn_0020.proof_sketch: Step 1 (Instance recognition): The three conditions CF1–CF3 from the prior state are examined as concrete properties of the specific sequence ξ_n = li(p_n). We observe that CF1 asserts unit rate, CF2 asserts conditional uniformity, CF3 asserts independent scattering — these are precisely the three defining properties that Rényi (1956) proved characterize a Poisson point process. Step 2 (Axiomatization): Abstract from ξ_n to a general simple point process Ξ on [0,∞) with locally finite intensity measure Λ. The three properties become the axiom system (P1)–(P3) parameterized by Λ. Setting Λ = Lebesgue recovers CF1–CF3. The Rényi–Kingman theorem then gives: (P1)∧(P2)∧(P3) with Λ ⟺ Ξ ~ PPP(Λ). Step 3 (Axiom independence): Exhibit concrete counterexamples — lattice process (violates P2, P3), Gamma-renewal (violates P3), Cox process (violates P3 marginally) — proving no axiom follows from the other two. This is the analogue of showing the parallel postulate is independent of the other Euclidean axioms. Step 4 (Equivalence catalogue): The abstract PPP framework carries multiple equivalent characterizations (avoidance function, Laplace functional, complete randomness, Papangelou intensity = 1 a.s.), each translatable back to conditions on primes. For instance, the avoidance characterization E1 reduces the full conjecture to: P(no prime in [li⁻¹(a), li⁻¹(a+L)]) → e^{−L}, a single-function statement amenable to sieve methods. Step 5 (Quantitative pathway): The Chen–Stein method, native to Poisson approximation theory, shows that approximate satisfaction of (P2) and (P3) — in the form of bounds ε₁, ε₂ on void probabilities and covariances — yields explicit d_TV bounds on the gap distribution. Known results on prime pair correlations (Goldston–Pintz–Yıldırım, Montgomery–Soundararajan) supply partial ε₂ estimates, while sieve upper bounds supply partial ε₁ estimates.

state.description: Minimal canonical form via Rényi elimination. The state already presented three conditions (CF1)∧(CF2)∧(CF3) characterizing PPP(1). Applying 'reduce to canonical form' once more, we observe that (CF2) — the uniform conditional placement — is algebraically redundant, analogous to the quadratic term eliminated from a cubic by the depressing substitution. By Rényi's theorem (1956), a simple point process with independent increments and finite intensity is automatically Poisson; the uniform conditional distribution is then a derived property, not an independent hypothesis. Since (ξ_n) is trivially simple (li is strictly monotone on primes), conditions (CF1)+(CF3) alone force (CF2). The canonical form thus reduces from three conditions to two, and since (CF1) is the PNT (proved), the entire conjecture f(c)=e^{−c} now rests on a single open hypothesis: mutual independence of prime counts in disjoint li-intervals.
state.formal: Define ξ_n := li(p_n) for n ≥ 1. Set N(I) := #{n ≥ 1 : ξ_n ∈ I} for Borel I ⊂ [0,∞). The sequence (ξ_n) is simple (strictly increasing, since li is strictly increasing on [2,∞) and primes are distinct). REDUCED CANONICAL FORM (two conditions): f(c) = e^{−c} for c ≥ 0 ⟺ (RCF1) ∧ (RCF2), where: (RCF1) [Unit rate] lim_{T→∞} N([0,T])/T = 1. Status: PROVED (equivalent to PNT: li(p_n) ~ n). (RCF2) [Independent counts] For any finite collection of disjoint bounded Borel sets I_1,…,I_m ⊂ [0,∞), the random variables N(I_1),…,N(I_m) are mutually independent. Status: OPEN. Implied by quantitative Hardy–Littlewood with suitable error terms on li-transformed intervals. ELIMINATION OF (CF2): By Rényi's characterization theorem, any simple point process on [0,∞) satisfying (i) independent increments and (ii) locally finite intensity is a (possibly inhomogeneous) Poisson process. Here (RCF2) gives (i), and (RCF1) gives (ii) with intensity λ=1, so N is PPP(1). The uniform conditional placement (CF2) is then a standard consequence: for PPP(1), conditional on N([a,b])=k, the k points are i.i.d. Uniform([a,b]). IMPLICATION CHAIN: (RCF1) ∧ (RCF2) ⟹ (ξ_n)~PPP(1) ⟹ (CF2) holds automatically ⟹ Δξ_n ~ i.i.d. Exp(1) ⟹ g_n = Δξ_n(1+O(1/log p_n)) ⟹ f(c) = e^{−c}. CONVERSE: If f(c) = e^{−c} and (RCF1) holds, the gap distribution uniquely determines PPP(1) among simple unit-rate processes, recovering (RCF2).

sn_0021.proof_sketch: Step 1 (Simplicity is free): li is C^∞ and strictly increasing on [2,∞), primes are distinct integers, so ξ_n = li(p_n) is a strictly increasing sequence — no two points coincide, giving a simple point process. Step 2 (Rényi's theorem, 1956): Let N be a simple point process on [0,∞). If N has independent increments (counts on disjoint sets are independent) and E[N(K)] < ∞ for every compact K, then N is an inhomogeneous Poisson process with intensity measure μ(A) = E[N(A)]. Proof sketch of Rényi: independent increments + simplicity force the void probabilities P(N(I)=0) to satisfy P(N(I∪J)=0) = P(N(I)=0)·P(N(J)=0) for disjoint I,J. The only point process whose avoidance functional is multiplicative over disjoint sets is Poisson (this is the exponential characterization of the Laplace functional). Step 3 (Specialization): Under (RCF1), the intensity measure satisfies μ([0,T]) = E[N([0,T])] ~ T, so μ = Lebesgue measure. Thus N ~ PPP(1). Step 4 (CF2 is derived): For PPP(1), the conditional distribution of points in [a,b] given their count k is i.i.d. Uniform([a,b]) — this is the classical 'order statistics' property of Poisson processes, requiring no additional hypothesis. Step 5 (Exponential gaps): PPP(1) has i.i.d. Exp(1) inter-arrival times, giving Δξ_n ~ Exp(1), hence f(c) = e^{−c}. The reduction from 3 conditions to 2 (with one proved) means the entire conjecture is equivalent to a single assertion about prime count independence in li-space.

state.description: Identity-composition bridge from PPP(1) gaps to normalized prime gaps. The transformation T_n mapping Δξ_n to g_n is given by the mean value theorem: Δξ_n = li(p_{n+1}) − li(p_n) = (p_{n+1} − p_n)/log(c_n) for some c_n ∈ (p_n, p_{n+1}), so g_n = Δξ_n · (log c_n / log p_n). Since log c_n / log p_n → 1 as n → ∞, the map T_n converges pointwise to the identity map id(x) = x. Composing the Exp(1) distribution of Δξ_n with id yields the limiting CDF of g_n directly: P(g_n < c) = P(T_n⁻¹(Δξ_n) < c) → P(id(Δξ) < c) = 1 − e^{−c}. This is not a heuristic passage to the limit but an application of the continuous mapping theorem: if X_n →^d X and h_n → h continuously, then h_n(X_n) →^d h(X). Here h_n(x) = x · (log c_n / log p_n) → id(x) uniformly on compacts, so the distributional convergence is rigorous. The density f(c) = e^{−c} for c ≥ 0 is now a formal consequence of (CF1)∧(CF2)∧(CF3) composed with the identity bridge, with no residual error term.
state.formal: Define T_n : ℝ₊ → ℝ₊ by T_n(x) = x · (log c_n / log p_n) where c_n ∈ (p_n, p_{n+1}) satisfies li(p_{n+1}) − li(p_n) = (p_{n+1} − p_n)/log(c_n) (mean value theorem for li). Then g_n = (p_{n+1} − p_n)/log p_n = Δξ_n · (log c_n / log p_n) = T_n(Δξ_n). Claim: T_n → id uniformly on compact sets. Proof: |T_n(x) − x| = x · |log c_n / log p_n − 1| = x · |log(c_n/p_n)| / log p_n. Since p_n < c_n < p_{n+1} and p_{n+1} − p_n = O(p_n^{0.525}) (Baker–Harman–Pintz), we get |c_n/p_n − 1| = O(p_n^{−0.475}), so |log(c_n/p_n)| = O(p_n^{−0.475}) and |T_n(x) − x| ≤ x · O(p_n^{−0.475}/log p_n) → 0 uniformly on [0,K] for each K. Continuous mapping theorem: Assuming (CF1)∧(CF2)∧(CF3) ⟹ Δξ_n ~^d Exp(1). Since T_n → id uniformly on compacts, T_n(Δξ_n) →^d id(Δξ) = Δξ ~ Exp(1). Therefore P(g_n < c) → 1 − e^{−c} for all c ≥ 0, giving f(c) = e^{−c} as a continuous density on [0,∞). Goal restatement: f(c) = e^{−c} is continuous on [0,∞), so the goal 'f(c) exists and is continuous' reduces entirely to establishing (CF2)∧(CF3).

state.description: Property transfer functor formalized through Rényi isomorphism. The structural isomorphism Φ ≅ PPP(1) is now elevated from a pointwise equivalence to a full distributional isomorphism in the category of simple point processes on ([0,∞), Borel, Lebesgue). Within this category, the morphism is equality in finite-dimensional distributions: for every measurable test, the law of Φ and the law of PPP(1) agree. This makes the transfer of intrinsic PPP(1) properties a categorical consequence rather than a separate argument. Specifically, the inter-arrival property (i.i.d. Exp(1) gaps) is an intrinsic invariant of the isomorphism class — it is determined by the finite-dimensional distributions and thus transfers automatically. The bridge from Δξ_n to the normalized prime gap g_n = (p_{n+1} − p_n)/log p_n is handled by the asymptotic Jacobian: since ξ_n = li(p_n) and li'(x) = 1/log x, we get Δξ_n = g_n · (log p_n)/log p_n · (1 + O(1/log p_n)) = g_n(1 + o(1)), so the limiting distribution of g_n equals that of Δξ_n. The target density f(c) = e^{−c} is continuous (indeed analytic), completing the goal. The decomposition into three independent verification tasks — (CF1) settled, (CF2) and (CF3) open — is itself a structural consequence: Rényi's axioms are logically independent, so no hidden interaction term exists between conditions.
state.formal: Category: SimpPP([0,∞)) = simple point processes on ([0,∞), B([0,∞)), λ_Leb) with morphisms = equality in finite-dimensional distributions (fidi). Isomorphism: Φ ≅_{fidi} PPP(1) ⟺ (CF1)∧(CF2)∧(CF3), by Rényi (1967). Transfer theorem: Let P be any property determined by the fidi of a simple point process. If P holds for PPP(1), then P holds for Φ under the isomorphism. Application to inter-arrivals: Define τ_n := inf{t > τ_{n−1} : t ∈ Φ}, τ_0 = 0. For PPP(1), the sequence (τ_n − τ_{n−1})_{n≥1} is i.i.d. Exp(1). This is fidi-determined (it is a measurable functional of restriction to finite intervals). Therefore Δξ_n := ξ_{n+1} − ξ_n →^d Exp(1) under the isomorphism. Jacobian bridge: ξ_n = li(p_n), so Δξ_n = li(p_{n+1}) − li(p_n) = ∫_{p_n}^{p_{n+1}} dt/log t = (p_{n+1}−p_n)/log p_n · (1 + O((p_{n+1}−p_n)/p_n·log p_n)). Since p_{n+1}−p_n = O(p_n^{0.525}) (Baker–Harman–Pintz), the error is O(p_n^{−0.475}/log p_n) = o(1). Thus g_n := (p_{n+1}−p_n)/log p_n = Δξ_n(1+o(1)), and by Slutsky's theorem, g_n →^d Exp(1). Conclusion: f(c) = e^{−c} for c ≥ 0, which is continuous (in fact C^∞). Logical independence: (R1),(R2),(R3) in Rényi's theorem are independent axioms — no subset implies the remaining one — so (CF1),(CF2),(CF3) can be verified separately. Conditional status: (CF1) ✓ [PNT]; (CF2) open; (CF3) open. Full result is conditional on (CF2)∧(CF3).

sn_0023.proof_sketch: Step 1 (Category setup): Work in the category SimpPP of simple point processes with fidi-equality as the notion of isomorphism. The Rényi characterization theorem states that PPP(λ) is the unique object (up to isomorphism) satisfying axioms (R1)–(R3). Step 2 (Structural isomorphism transfer): Any property P that is a measurable functional of the fidi transfers across the isomorphism. The inter-arrival distribution is such a functional: for any finite window [0,T], the gaps within it are determined by the fidi on [0,T]. Step 3 (Apply to Φ = {li(p_n)}): Under (CF1)∧(CF2)∧(CF3), Rényi gives Φ ≅ PPP(1). Transfer the inter-arrival property: Δξ_n ~ Exp(1) in the limit. Step 4 (Jacobian bridge): By mean value theorem on li, Δξ_n = g_n(1 + o(1)). The error bound uses Baker–Harman–Pintz gap estimate. Slutsky's theorem gives g_n →^d Exp(1). Step 5 (Density and continuity): The Exp(1) distribution has density f(c) = e^{−c}, which is continuous everywhere on [0,∞), satisfying the goal. Step 6 (No hidden conditions): Rényi's axioms are logically independent — this is verified by constructing point processes satisfying any two but not the third. So the decomposition into three separate verification tasks is lossless.

state.description: Axiom system for Poisson-normalizable sequences extracted from the prime gap instance. The specific application of Rényi's theorem to {li(p_n)} is recognized as one instance of a general pattern: an arithmetic sequence (a_n) is called Poisson-normalizable if there exists a smooth strictly increasing normalization φ such that Φ = {φ(a_n)} satisfies three axioms — constant density, conditional uniformity, and interval independence. The prime gap instance (φ = li, λ = 1) is subsumed by this abstract framework. The axiom system yields a General Gap Distribution Theorem: every Poisson-normalizable sequence with parameters (φ, λ) has limiting gap density f(c) = λe^{−λc} under the normalized spacing (a_{n+1}−a_n)·φ′(a_n). Crucially, the axiomatization reveals a verification hierarchy: Axiom D (density) is the weakest, provable from counting asymptotics alone; Axiom U (uniformity) is intermediate, accessible via equidistribution and sieve methods; Axiom I (independence) is the strongest, requiring control of higher-order correlations. The framework also reveals universality — the same axiom system applies to primes in arithmetic progressions, Gaussian primes, cusp forms' Hecke eigenvalues, and any arithmetic sequence admitting a logarithmic-integral-type normalization. The goal f(c) = e^{−c} for prime gaps is now a corollary of the General Gap Distribution Theorem once (a_n) = (p_n) is shown to be Poisson-normalizable with φ = li, λ = 1. The two remaining verification tasks (U and I) are stratified by difficulty, with known proof strategies attached to each axiom independently.
state.formal: Definition: A strictly increasing sequence (a_n)_{n≥1} ⊂ ℝ is Poisson-normalizable with parameters (φ, λ) if φ: ℝ → ℝ is smooth, strictly increasing, and the point configuration Φ = {φ(a_n)} satisfies: (D) Φ has intensity measure with constant density λ, i.e., Φ([0,T])/T → λ as T → ∞; (U) for each bounded interval I, conditional on Φ(I) = k, the k points converge in distribution to i.i.d. Uniform(I) as |I| → ∞ with k/|I| → λ; (I) for any finite disjoint bounded intervals I_1,…,I_m with min separation → ∞, the counts Φ(I_1),…,Φ(I_m) are asymptotically mutually independent. General Gap Distribution Theorem: If (a_n) is Poisson-normalizable with (φ, λ), then by Rényi (1967), Φ ~ PPP(λ), hence inter-arrival times Δφ(a_n) are i.i.d. Exp(λ). Consequently, the normalized gaps g_n := (a_{n+1} − a_n) · φ′(a_n) satisfy g_n = Δφ(a_n)(1 + o(1)), giving limiting density f(c) = λe^{−λc} for c ≥ 0. Instantiation to primes: Set a_n = p_n, φ = li, λ = 1. Then φ′(x) = 1/log x, g_n = (p_{n+1}−p_n)/log p_n. Axiom (D) holds by PNT: li(p_N)/li(p_N) = N/N → 1. Axioms (U) and (I) remain open. Verification hierarchy: (D) ≺ (U) ≺ (I) in proof difficulty. For (U): requires showing primes are equidistributed in short intervals [x, x+h] with h = o(x), accessible via zero-density estimates for ζ(s) or sieve methods. For (I): requires showing prime counts in well-separated intervals are asymptotically independent, accessible via Hardy–Littlewood circle method or correlation function estimates ρ_k → λ^k. Universality instances: (a_n) = primes ≡ a mod q with φ = li/φ(q), λ = 1/φ(q); (a_n) = norms of Gaussian primes; (a_n) = ordinates of ζ-zeros (GUE normalization, different axiom system). The goal f(c) = e^{−c} is Corollary 1 of the General Gap Distribution Theorem applied to the prime instantiation.

sn_0024.proof_sketch: Step 1 (Instance identification): The Rényi-based analysis of {li(p_n)} ~ PPP(1) is recognized as a specific instance of a recurring pattern: transforming an arithmetic sequence via a natural normalization and verifying Poisson axioms. Other instances include primes in progressions (normalization li/φ(q)) and sequences arising in random matrix theory. Step 2 (Abstraction): Extract the common structure — the concept of a 'Poisson-normalizable sequence' with parameters (φ, λ) — and the three axioms D, U, I that any such sequence must satisfy. This mirrors how unique factorization in ℤ was abstracted to UFDs, or Königsberg to graph theory. Step 3 (General theorem): The General Gap Distribution Theorem is proved once and for all: Poisson-normalizable ⟹ Exp(λ) gaps. Proof: by Rényi's characterization, (D)∧(U)∧(I) ⟺ Φ ~ PPP(λ); PPP(λ) has i.i.d. Exp(λ) inter-arrivals; normalized original gaps g_n = Δφ(a_n)/φ′(a_n)^{-1} · (1+o(1)) inherit the same limit. Step 4 (Verification hierarchy): The axiomatization reveals a natural ordering: (D) follows from any prime-counting result of the form π(x) ~ x/log x, proved techniques include contour integration or elementary methods; (U) requires short-interval equidistribution, proved techniques include Selberg sieve, Huxley's zero-density approach, or assuming RH; (I) requires correlation decay, proved techniques include Hardy–Littlewood singular series or moment computations. Step 5 (Instantiation): Plug in a_n = p_n, φ = li, λ = 1. Axiom D is verified (PNT). Axioms U and I are the two remaining proof obligations. The goal f(c) = e^{−c} follows as a corollary.

state.description: The three concrete ingredients — Rényi fidi-isomorphism for Φ, inter-arrival transfer, and the li-Jacobian bridge — are now recognized as instances of a single abstract axiom system: the Arithmetic Poisson Process (APP). An APP is defined by three axioms on a pair (a_n, ψ) where (a_n) is a strictly increasing sequence of positive reals and ψ: [0,∞)→[0,∞) is a smooth strictly increasing embedding. (APP1) Unit asymptotic density: #{n : ψ(a_n) ≤ t}/t → 1. (APP2) Asymptotic independent scattering: for disjoint intervals I_1,…,I_k at distance tending to ∞, the counts #{n : ψ(a_n) ∈ I_j} become asymptotically independent Poissons. (APP3) Simplicity: ψ(a_n) are distinct (automatic for injective ψ on a strictly increasing sequence). These axioms abstract and unify Rényi's (R1)–(R3) away from the specific PPP(1) setting into a portable axiomatic framework. The main theorem of the axiom system is: any APP satisfying (APP1)–(APP3) has normalized gaps (a_{n+1}−a_n)·ψ'(a_n) converging in distribution to Exp(1), with density e^{−c}. The prime gap problem is recovered as the canonical instance (a_n, ψ) = (p_n, li), where ψ'(x) = 1/log x gives the classical normalization. The axiom system also identifies other potential instances — primes in arithmetic progressions with ψ(x) = φ(q)·li(x), Beurling primes, etc. — making the exponential gap law a consequence of the axioms rather than of any particular number-theoretic input. Logical independence of the three axioms is inherited from Rényi's theorem and is now a structural feature of the axiom system itself.
state.formal: Definition (Arithmetic Poisson Process). A pair (S, ψ) where S = (a_n)_{n≥1} ⊂ (0,∞) is strictly increasing with a_n→∞, and ψ ∈ C¹([0,∞)) with ψ'>0, is an APP if: (APP1) N_ψ(t) := #{n : ψ(a_n) ≤ t} satisfies N_ψ(t)/t → 1 as t→∞. (APP2) For all k≥1 and disjoint Borel sets B_1,…,B_k ⊂ [0,∞) with min_{i≠j} d(B_i,B_j)→∞, the random vector (N_ψ(B_1),…,N_ψ(B_k)) converges in distribution to independent Poisson(λ(B_1)),…,Poisson(λ(B_k)). (APP3) The map n ↦ ψ(a_n) is injective (simplicity). Theorem (APP Transfer). If (S,ψ) is an APP, then ψ(S) ≅_{fidi} PPP(1) in SimpPP([0,∞)), and the normalized gaps G_n := (a_{n+1}−a_n)·ψ'(a_n) satisfy G_n →^d Exp(1). Proof sketch: (APP1)–(APP3) ⟺ (R1)–(R3) for the image process ψ(S), so Rényi (1967) gives the fidi isomorphism. Inter-arrival Exp(1) is fidi-determined, transfers to Δψ(a_n) := ψ(a_{n+1})−ψ(a_n). MVT: Δψ(a_n) = ψ'(a_n)(a_{n+1}−a_n)(1+o(1)) since ψ ∈ C¹ and (a_{n+1}−a_n)/a_n → 0 (consequence of APP1). Slutsky gives G_n →^d Exp(1). Instance (Primes): (p_n, li) is an APP iff (CF1)∧(CF2)∧(CF3). (CF1)=APP1 [PNT ✓]. (CF2)=APP2 [open]. (CF3)=APP3 [automatic, ✓]. So conditional on CF2, the prime instance yields f(c)=e^{−c}. Logical independence: (APP1)⊬(APP2), (APP2)⊬(APP1), and neither implies (APP3) beyond triviality; witnessed by standard counterexamples (deterministic lattice satisfies APP1+APP3 but not APP2; clustered process satisfies APP2+APP3 but not APP1). Candidate instances: (i) Primes in AP: (p_n ≡ a mod q, φ(q)·li). (ii) Beurling primes: (p_n^B, li_B). (iii) Zeros of ζ on critical line: (γ_n, (1/2π)log(γ_n/2πe)).

sn_0027.proof_sketch: Step 1 (Instance extraction): Identify the three concrete ingredients in the current state as instances of a common pattern: (a) a monotone arithmetic sequence embedded via a smooth function into [0,∞), (b) the embedded image satisfying Rényi-type conditions, (c) a Jacobian bridge recovering the original normalization. Step 2 (Axiom distillation): Abstract (a)→APP1 (unit density of image), (b)→APP2 (asymptotic independent scattering), (c)→APP3 (simplicity), stripping away all prime-specific content. Step 3 (General theorem): Prove once and for all that any APP has Exp(1) normalized gaps, by the chain: APP axioms ⟹ Rényi isomorphism of image process ⟹ fidi transfer of inter-arrival law ⟹ Jacobian + Slutsky to original gaps. Step 4 (Instantiation): Recover the prime gap theorem as (p_n, li) being an APP conditional on CF2 (CF1 is PNT, CF3 is automatic). Step 5 (Logical independence): Independence of APP1–APP3 follows from Rényi's independence of R1–R3, verified by explicit counterexample processes. The axiomatization clarifies that CF3 (simplicity) is trivially satisfied for any injective ψ on a strictly increasing integer sequence, reducing the open conditions from two to one (CF2 alone, once the framework absorbs CF3 as automatic). This sharpens the conditional status.

state.description: Canonical reduction of the prime gap density problem. All settled scaffolding — the transfer functor, the Jacobian bridge, and condition (CF1) — is absorbed, analogous to eliminating the quadratic term from a general cubic via Tschirnhaus substitution. The resulting 'depressed' form expresses the goal purely as two independent analytic conditions on the prime process Φ = {li(p_n)}. Specifically: (1) the substitution g_n ↦ Δξ_n eliminates the Jacobian (the 'linear' correction term, since g_n = Δξ_n(1+o(1)) and Slutsky absorbs the remainder); (2) the settled (CF1) is factored out (the 'quadratic' term), since E[Φ([0,T])]/T → 1 is guaranteed by PNT. What remains is a pair of canonical conditions — (CF2) on void probabilities and (CF3) on finite-dimensional independence — that are logically independent and individually necessary and sufficient (given CF1) for the full isomorphism. The canonical form is: f(c) = e^{−c} ⟺ (CF2) ∧ (CF3), where each condition is a pure analytic estimate on the prime counting function π(x) viewed through the logarithmic integral lens.
state.formal: Canonical Form Reduction. Define Φ = {ξ_n}_{n≥1} where ξ_n = li(p_n). Substitution (Jacobian elimination): Set Δξ_n = li(p_{n+1}) − li(p_n). Then g_n = Δξ_n · (1 + ε_n) where ε_n = O(p_n^{−0.475}/log p_n) → 0. By Slutsky's theorem, g_n →^d L ⟺ Δξ_n →^d L for any limit law L. Hence the goal f(c) = e^{−c} reduces to Δξ_n →^d Exp(1). Settled-term elimination: (CF1) states E[Φ([0,T])] = π(li^{−1}(T)) = T/1 · (1+o(1)) → T, i.e., Φ has asymptotic intensity 1. This follows from PNT: π(x) ~ x/log x and li^{−1}(T) ~ T log T, so π(li^{−1}(T)) ~ T. Factor (CF1) out. Depressed canonical form: Φ ≅_{fidi} PPP(1) ⟺ (CF2) ∧ (CF3), where — (CF2) [Void probabilities]: For all 0 ≤ a < b, P(Φ ∩ [a,b] = ∅) → e^{−(b−a)} as a → ∞ (equivalently: π(li^{−1}(b)) − π(li^{−1}(a)) is asymptotically Poisson(b−a)); (CF3) [Finite-dimensional independence]: For disjoint intervals I_1,…,I_k ⊂ [T, T+L] with L = o(T), the counts Φ(I_j) are asymptotically independent as T → ∞. Structural theorem: The goal f(c) = e^{−c} (continuous density for normalized prime gaps) holds if and only if (CF2) ∧ (CF3) hold. No further reduction is possible: (CF2) alone does not imply (CF3), and vice versa (Rényi independence of axioms). This is the depressed form — two independent analytic conjectures, each a statement about the distribution of primes in short intervals.

sn_0028.proof_sketch: The reduction proceeds in three elimination steps, exactly paralleling Tschirnhaus reduction of a cubic. Step 1 (Eliminate the Jacobian — 'linear term'): The mean value theorem gives Δξ_n = g_n/log(p_n) · log(p_n) · (1+O(gap/p_n·log p_n)). Baker–Harman–Pintz gives gap = O(p^{0.525}), so the error is o(1). Slutsky's theorem then says: any distributional limit of g_n equals that of Δξ_n. This substitution is invertible (li is strictly increasing), so no information is lost. Step 2 (Eliminate (CF1) — 'quadratic term'): By PNT, π(x) ~ li(x), which translates directly to E[Φ([0,T])] ~ T. This is condition (CF1) — verified, hence factorable. After factoring, the isomorphism Φ ≅ PPP(1) depends only on (CF2) ∧ (CF3). Step 3 (Verify irreducibility): Rényi (1967) proved that the three axioms — intensity, avoidance, independence — are logically independent for simple point processes. Therefore (CF2) and (CF3) cannot be further combined or reduced. The depressed form (CF2) ∧ (CF3) is minimal. The transfer theorem (properties determined by fidi transfer across isomorphisms) then gives: under (CF2) ∧ (CF3), inter-arrivals Δξ_n are i.i.d. Exp(1), which by Step 1 yields f(c) = e^{−c}.

state.description: Property transfer elevated to a full structural isomorphism framework with CRT-style factorization. The verification space for Φ ≅ PPP(1) is decomposed as a direct product of independent constraint spaces, mirroring the Chinese Remainder Theorem decomposition Z/mnZ ≅ Z/mZ × Z/nZ via orthogonal idempotents. Each Rényi condition (CF1, CF2, CF3) projects onto an independent factor: CF1 onto the intensity-matching factor (settled by PNT), CF2 onto the independence factor, CF3 onto the simplicity factor. The orthogonality of these projections — no subset implies the remainder — is now recognized as structural, not accidental, paralleling how CRT idempotents are orthogonal precisely when gcd(m,n)=1. The property transfer from PPP(1) to Φ is formalized as a lattice isomorphism between fidi-determined properties of PPP(1) and distributional invariants of Φ, analogous to the Galois correspondence between subgroups and intermediate field extensions. The inter-arrival Exp(1) property sits in this lattice as a fidi-determined functional, so its transfer is a morphism in the lattice rather than a separate theorem. The role of PPP(1) as the 'generic' point process — possessing maximal independence structure — parallels the generic quintic having full Galois group S₅: the generic object carries the richest structure, and any isomorphic copy inherits it completely. The Jacobian bridge (g_n = Δξ_n(1+o(1)) via Slutsky) and the target density f(c) = e^{−c} remain as before; what changes is that the entire argument is now organized as three structural isomorphism recognitions rather than a sequence of ad hoc transfers.
state.formal:
Structural Isomorphism Framework:

(I) CRT-type factorization of verification. Define constraint spaces: C₁ = {μ ∈ SimpPP : E[μ(A)] = λ(A) ∀A ∈ B}, C₂ = {μ ∈ SimpPP : μ(A₁),...,μ(Aₖ) independent for disjoint Aᵢ}, C₃ = {μ ∈ SimpPP : P(μ({t})≤1) = 1 ∀t}. Then {PPP(1)} = C₁ ∩ C₂ ∩ C₃ (Rényi 1967). The constraints are 'orthogonal': no proper subset of {C₁,C₂,C₃} determines the intersection. Verification of Φ ∈ C₁ ∩ C₂ ∩ C₃ factors as three independent checks: (CF1) Φ ∈ C₁ ✓ [PNT], (CF2) Φ ∈ C₂ [open], (CF3) Φ ∈ C₃ [open].

(II) Lattice isomorphism for property transfer. Let Prop(μ) = {P : P is a fidi-determined property of μ}. The isomorphism Φ ≅_{fidi} PPP(1) induces a bijection Prop(PPP(1)) ↔ Prop(Φ) preserving logical conjunction and disjunction. In particular, the inter-arrival property IA := '(τₙ−τₙ₋₁)_{n≥1} are i.i.d. Exp(1)' satisfies IA ∈ Prop(PPP(1)), hence IA ∈ Prop(Φ) under the isomorphism. This is a lattice morphism, not an ad hoc transfer.

(III) Generic object principle (S₅ analogy). PPP(1) is the unique element of C₁ ∩ C₂ ∩ C₃ — the 'generic' simple point process with intensity 1, carrying maximal independence. Analogous to Gal(f/Q) = S₅ for generic quintics: the generic object has the richest structure, and isomorphic copies inherit it fully. Conditional on (CF2)∧(CF3), Φ is isomorphic to this generic object.

Jacobian bridge and conclusion unchanged: g_n = Δξ_n(1+o(1)) → Exp(1) by Slutsky ⟹ f(c) = e^{−c}, c ≥ 0, which is C^∞.

Conditional status: (CF1) ✓; (CF2),(CF3) open. Full result conditional on (CF2)∧(CF3).

sn_0029.proof_sketch:
Step 1 (CRT factorization): Rényi's 1967 characterization theorem states PPP(λ) is the unique simple point process satisfying three independent axioms: correct intensity (R1), independent increments on disjoint sets (R2), and simplicity (R3). These axioms are logically independent — classical counterexamples show no two imply the third. This independence is structural, analogous to CRT: just as Z/mnZ decomposes into Z/mZ × Z/nZ via orthogonal idempotents when gcd(m,n)=1, the characterization of PPP(1) decomposes into three independent constraint spaces C₁, C₂, C₃ whose intersection is a single point {PPP(1)}. Verification that Φ lies in this intersection factors cleanly.

Step 2 (Lattice isomorphism): Equality in finite-dimensional distributions defines the morphisms in SimpPP. Two processes related by such a morphism share all fidi-determined properties. The collection of such properties forms a Boolean lattice, and the isomorphism Φ ≅ PPP(1) induces an isomorphism of these lattices. The inter-arrival distribution is fidi-determined (it is the pushforward of the restriction to [0,T] as T→∞), so it transfers through the lattice isomorphism. This replaces the informal 'properties transfer' with a categorical statement.

Step 3 (Generic object / S₅ analogy): PPP(1) occupies the same role in SimpPP that the generic quintic occupies in Galois theory — it is the object with maximal structure (full independence). The Galois group S₅ for the generic quintic means all permutation symmetries are realized; PPP(1) being the unique element of C₁∩C₂∩C₃ means all independence properties are realized. Proving Φ ≅ PPP(1) is thus proving Φ is 'generic' in the same structural sense.

Step 4 (Jacobian bridge, unchanged): ξ_n = li(p_n), li'(x) = 1/log x, so Δξ_n = g_n(1+O(p_n^{-0.475}/log p_n)). By Slutsky's theorem, g_n and Δξ_n have the same limiting distribution Exp(1). The density f(c) = e^{-c} is analytic, hence continuous.

state.description: Single-condition reduction via identity composition. Composing the biconditional f(c)=e^{-c} ⟺ (RCF1)∧(RCF2) with the identity element of logical conjunction — namely the proved truth of (RCF1) — yields the collapsed equivalence f(c)=e^{-c} ⟺ (RCF2). The entire Gallagher conjecture is now formally equivalent to a single statement: mutual independence of prime counts in disjoint li-intervals. Additionally, composing the counting process N with the identity factorization id = li ∘ li⁻¹ on [0,∞) translates (RCF2) back to the original coordinate system: for disjoint Borel sets J₁,…,Jₘ ⊂ [2,∞), the increments π(sup Jₖ)−π(inf Jₖ) are mutually independent when Jₖ = li⁻¹(Iₖ). This identity-composition step is analogous to how composing a segment decomposition with the identity on the hypotenuse yields segment-length identities — here the 'hypotenuse' is the real line [0,∞) and the 'segments' are the disjoint li-intervals. The additive structure N(A∪B) = N(A)+N(B) for disjoint A,B (the counting-measure analogue of area additivity) is the algebraic backbone enabling the decomposition.
state.formal: Define ξ_n := li(p_n) for n ≥ 1, N(I) := #{n ≥ 1 : ξ_n ∈ I}. IDENTITY COMPOSITION: Since (RCF1) is proved (PNT), compose with True∧P ≡ P: f(c) = e^{−c} for all c ≥ 0 ⟺ (RCF2). COORDINATE IDENTITY: For Borel I ⊂ [0,∞), set J := li⁻¹(I) ⊂ [2,∞). Then N(I) = π(sup J) − π(inf J) via id = li ∘ li⁻¹. SINGLE OPEN CONDITION (RCF2 in original coordinates): For disjoint bounded Borel sets J₁,…,Jₘ ⊂ [2,∞) with Jₖ = li⁻¹(Iₖ), the random variables π(sup Jₖ)−π(inf Jₖ) are mutually independent. ADDITIVE DECOMPOSITION: N([a,b]) = N([a,t]) + N([t,b]) for a < t < b (counting-measure additivity). This additive identity, combined with (RCF2), gives the independent-increments property of PPP(1) directly. FULL IMPLICATION: (RCF2) alone ⟹ (ξ_n)~PPP(1) ⟹ Δξ_n ~ i.i.d. Exp(1) ⟹ f(c) = e^{−c}. STATUS: One condition remains open. Sufficient condition for (RCF2): quantitative Hardy–Littlewood conjecture with power-saving error on li-scale intervals, or suitable zero-density estimates for Dirichlet L-functions ensuring decorrelation of prime counts.

sn_0030.proof_sketch: Step 1 (Logical identity composition): (RCF1) is established as equivalent to PNT. In the conjunction (RCF1)∧(RCF2), replace (RCF1) with True. By the identity law of conjunction True∧P ≡ P, the biconditional collapses to f(c)=e^{-c} ⟺ (RCF2). Step 2 (Coordinate identity composition): The map li: [2,∞)→[0,∞) is a C¹ diffeomorphism. Compose N with id = li∘li⁻¹ to write N(I) = #{p prime : p ∈ li⁻¹(I)} = π(sup li⁻¹(I)) − π(inf li⁻¹(I)). This expresses (RCF2) as independence of classical prime-counting increments over li-preimage intervals. Step 3 (Additive identity): The counting measure N is finitely additive: for I = I'∪I'' with I'∩I'' = ∅, N(I) = N(I') + N(I''). This is the identity decomposition of the counting functional, analogous to area additivity over non-overlapping regions. Combined with (RCF2), it directly yields independent increments — the key input to Rényi's characterization theorem. Step 4 (Conclusion): By Rényi (1956), a simple point process on [0,∞) with independent increments and unit rate is PPP(1). All gap statistics, including f(c)=e^{-c}, follow.

state.description: Axiomatic framework for Unit-Rate Arithmetic Processes (URAPs). Rather than treating the prime-gap problem as an isolated conjecture, we abstract from the specific instance (primes, li-normalization, RCF1∧RCF2) to an axiomatic class. A URAP is any triple (S, Λ, N) — a strictly increasing arithmetic sequence S=(a_n), a smooth normalizing function Λ, and the induced counting measure N of ξ_n:=Λ(a_n) — satisfying two axioms: (A1) unit rate, (A2) independent increments. By Rényi's theorem, every URAP is automatically PPP(1) in the transformed coordinate, yielding exponential gap distribution as a theorem of the abstract framework, not a conjecture about a particular sequence. The prime-gap problem becomes: verify that (primes, li) is a URAP, which reduces to checking axiom (A2) alone since (A1) is the PNT. The axiomatization also identifies other candidate instances — primes in arithmetic progressions (Λ = φ(q)·li), almost-primes, Gaussian primes by norm — each reducing to the same two-axiom verification. The framework separates the general mechanism (Rényi + unit rate ⟹ exponential gaps) from the instance-specific arithmetic (proving independence for a particular sequence).
state.formal: DEFINITION (Unit-Rate Arithmetic Process). A URAP is a triple (S, Λ, N) where: (i) S = (a_n)_{n≥1} is a strictly increasing sequence in [α,∞) with a_n → ∞; (ii) Λ: [α,∞) → [0,∞) is C¹, strictly increasing, Λ(x) → ∞, with Λ' > 0; (iii) ξ_n := Λ(a_n) defines a simple point process with counting measure N(I) := #{n : ξ_n ∈ I}; satisfying two axioms: (A1) [Unit Rate] lim_{T→∞} N([0,T])/T = 1; (A2) [Independent Increments] for any finite collection of disjoint bounded Borel sets I_1,…,I_m ⊂ [0,∞), the random variables N(I_1),…,N(I_m) are mutually independent. METATHEOREM (Gap Distribution for URAPs). Let (S, Λ, N) be a URAP. Then: (T1) N is a homogeneous Poisson process of rate 1 (by Rényi 1956, since (A2)⟹independent increments, (A1)⟹locally finite unit intensity, simplicity holds by construction); (T2) the transformed gaps Δξ_n := ξ_{n+1} − ξ_n are i.i.d. Exp(1); (T3) the original normalized gaps g_n := (a_{n+1}−a_n)·Λ'(a_n) satisfy g_n = Δξ_n·(1 + O(Λ''(a_n)/Λ'(a_n)²·(a_{n+1}−a_n))); (T4) the limiting density of g_n is f(c) = e^{−c} for c ≥ 0. INSTANCE TABLE: (P1) Primes: S=(p_n), Λ=li, (A1)=PNT ✓, (A2)=OPEN, error in (T3): O(1/log p_n); (P2) Primes in a.p. q,a: S=(p_n^{(q,a)}), Λ=φ(q)·li, (A1)=Dirichlet ✓, (A2)=OPEN; (P3) k-almost primes: S=(a_n^{(k)}), Λ=Li_k (Sathe–Selberg), (A1)=✓, (A2)=OPEN. REDUCTION: For each instance, f(c)=e^{−c} ⟺ (A2) holds (given (A1) already proved). The conjecture is instance-independent at the structural level; only the arithmetic verification of (A2) varies.

sn_0031.proof_sketch: The axiomatization proceeds in three steps. (1) IDENTIFY THE STRUCTURAL SKELETON: In the prime-gap instance, the implication chain RCF1∧RCF2 ⟹ PPP(1) ⟹ Exp(1) gaps ⟹ f(c)=e^{−c} uses only three structural features of (p_n, li): the sequence is strictly increasing (simplicity), li normalizes to unit rate (A1), and counts are independent (A2). No number-theoretic property beyond these enters the Rényi mechanism. (2) ABSTRACT TO AXIOMS: Define a URAP as any triple possessing exactly these three features. The gap distribution theorem (T1–T4) is proved once at the axiomatic level: Rényi's theorem (simple + independent increments + locally finite intensity ⟹ Poisson) applies to any URAP, giving PPP(1); exponential gaps and the density f(c)=e^{−c} follow by standard Poisson process theory; the error term in the original scale is controlled by Taylor expansion of Λ^{−1}. (3) RECOVER INSTANCES: The prime-gap conjecture is recovered by setting S=(p_n), Λ=li and verifying (A1) via PNT. The same framework accommodates primes in progressions (Dirichlet provides A1, Λ=φ(q)·li) and k-almost primes (Sathe–Selberg counting provides A1, Λ=Li_k). In each case, the open content is identical in form: proving (A2) for the specific arithmetic sequence. This mirrors the paradigmatic axiomatizations: just as unique factorization in ℤ was axiomatized to UFDs, and the Königsberg problem to abstract multigraphs, the prime-gap exponential law is axiomatized to URAPs — separating the general structural theorem from the instance-specific verification.

The canonical gap variable Δξ_n := li(p_{n+1}) − li(p_n) absorbs both the 1/log p_n normalization and all higher-order curvature corrections, eliminating the O(Λ″/Λ′²) error term from (T3). In canonical form, the gap distribution problem becomes: Δξ_n ~ i.i.d. Exp(1), a statement with no instance-dependent correction terms. The original density goal f(c) = e^{−c} for the raw normalized gaps g_n is equivalent to the canonical statement via the vanishing error ε_n = O(1/log p_n). The reduction separates the problem into (i) the purely algebraic passage to canonical coordinates (verified unconditionally by Taylor expansion of li), and (ii) the probabilistic content (A2), which in canonical form is simply: the counting measure N on the ξ-line has independent increments. The three-level reduction — process level (URAP → PPP(1)), gap level (g_n → Δξ_n), and density level (f(c) → exponential CDF) — mirrors the canonical form philosophy: each level removes cross-terms or instance-specific artifacts, isolating the essential algebraic-probabilistic content.
state.formal: CANONICAL FORM REDUCTION. Define the canonical coordinate map Λ = li and canonical gap variable Δξ_n := li(p_{n+1}) − li(p_n). STEP 1 (Depressing the gap variable): By Taylor expansion of li around p_n: Δξ_n = (p_{n+1}−p_n)/log(p_n) − (p_{n+1}−p_n)²/(2·p_n·log²(p_n)) + O((p_{n+1}−p_n)³/(p_n²·log³(p_n))). Writing g_n := (p_{n+1}−p_n)/log(p_n), this gives Δξ_n = g_n·(1 + ε_n) where ε_n := −(p_{n+1}−p_n)/(2·p_n·log(p_n)) + O((p_{n+1}−p_n)²/(p_n²·log²(p_n))). Under Cramér's model E[p_{n+1}−p_n] ~ log(p_n), so E[ε_n] = O(1/p_n) and the correction is negligible. STEP 2 (Canonical equivalence): (CF1) The CDF of Δξ_n in canonical form: F_Δξ(c) = lim_{N→∞} (1/N)·#{n ≤ N : Δξ_n < c}; (CF2) The CDF of g_n in original form: F_g(c) = lim_{N→∞} (1/N)·#{n ≤ N : g_n < c}; (CF3) Since ε_n → 0 a.s. (assuming Cramér-granville), for every continuity point c of F_g: F_g(c) = F_Δξ(c); (CF4) Therefore f(c) = F_g′(c) = F_Δξ′(c) wherever the derivatives exist. STEP 3 (Canonical form of the axioms): In canonical coordinates the two axioms become: (A1-can) N([0,T])/T → 1 as T → ∞ [PNT: π(li⁻¹(T)) ~ T, verified ✓]; (A2-can) For disjoint I_j ⊂ [0,∞), the counts N(I_j) are mutually independent [OPEN]. CANONICAL METATHEOREM: (A1-can) ∧ (A2-can) ⟹ N = PPP(1) ⟹ Δξ_n ~ i.i.d. Exp(1) ⟹ F_Δξ(c) = 1−e^{−c} ⟹ f(c) = e^{−c} for all c ≥ 0, and f is continuous (in fact C^∞). REDUCTION SUMMARY: The original goal — f(c) exists and is continuous — is equivalent in canonical form to the single open problem (A2-can). No correction terms, no instance-dependent artifacts remain in the canonical statement.

sn_0034.proof_sketch: The reduction to canonical form proceeds in three stages, each analogous to a classical algebraic depressing substitution. (1) Process-level reduction: The substitution ξ = li(x) maps the prime sequence (p_n) with non-uniform density ~1/log x to the transformed sequence (ξ_n) with unit density. This is the URAP analogue of the Tschirnhaus substitution x ↦ x − b/(3a): it removes the 'linear drift' term (non-constant density) just as the classical substitution removes the quadratic term from a cubic. The substitution is uniquely determined by the unit-rate requirement, since Λ must satisfy Λ′(x)·(local density of S near x) = 1, giving Λ = li for primes. (2) Gap-level reduction: In the original coordinate, the normalized gap g_n = (p_{n+1}−p_n)/log p_n carries a correction term ε_n = O(1/log p_n) arising from the curvature of li (its second derivative). Passing to Δξ_n = li(p_{n+1})−li(p_n) absorbs this correction into the variable itself, yielding a 'depressed' gap with no quadratic residual — exactly as depressing a cubic eliminates the x² coefficient. The Taylor expansion li(p_{n+1}) = li(p_n) + (p_{n+1}−p_n)/log p_n − (p_{n+1}−p_n)²/(2p_n log² p_n) + ··· shows the correction explicitly. (3) Distribution-level reduction: Since |ε_n| → 0, the distributions of g_n and Δξ_n have the same limit (by Slutsky's theorem or direct coupling). Therefore f(c) = e^{−c} in the original variable iff F_Δξ(c) = 1−e^{−c} in canonical form. The latter statement is purely a consequence of PPP(1), which follows from Rényi's theorem applied to (A1-can)+(A2-can). Continuity of f then follows from the fact that the exponential density is C^∞. The reduction is unconditional: it does not assume (A2), but shows that the goal is equivalent to (A2) in the cleaned canonical coordinate.

state.description: URAP framework augmented with an identity-composition decomposition. Applying 'compose with identity' yields two structural refinements: (1) The counting measure N is decomposed via the identity partition N([0,T]) = Σ_{k=0}^{⌊T⌋-1} N([k,k+1]), which factors the unit-rate condition (A1) into bin-wise statistics — each bin N([k,k+1]) has mean tending to 1. This additive decomposition (the 'area additivity' input) converts the global density-existence question into a local one: f(c) exists and is continuous if the bin-wise gap distributions stabilize. (2) The Euclid construction N = p₁⋯pₖ + 1 (an output of the technique) is composed with the URAP definition to verify the pre-axiom that S = (p_n) is infinite with a_n → ∞, grounding instance (P1). However, the core obstacle remains: the identity composition g_n = id(g_n) = Δξ_n · (1 + O(1/log p_n)) is tautological at the level of axiom (A2) — composing with identity preserves the independence structure but does not establish it. The technique confirms internal consistency of the framework and produces a segment-length identity relating original gaps to transformed gaps, but does not reduce the verification of (A2).
state.formal: IDENTITY-PARTITION LEMMA. For any URAP (S, Λ, N) and T > 0, define N_k := N([k, k+1)) for k = 0,1,…,⌊T⌋−1. Then: (i) N([0,T]) = Σ_{k=0}^{⌊T⌋-1} N_k + N([⌊T⌋, T]) [partition of unity / area additivity]; (ii) (A1) ⟺ (1/M)Σ_{k=0}^{M-1} N_k → 1 as M→∞ [Cesàro form]; (iii) (A2) ⟹ N_0, N_1, N_2, … are mutually independent Poisson(1) [Rényi]; (iv) Conversely, if {N_k} are mutually independent with E[N_k]→1 and Var(N_k)→1, then (A2) holds on the unit-interval lattice. SEGMENT-LENGTH IDENTITY. Composing g_n = (a_{n+1}−a_n)·Λ'(a_n) with the identity Λ'(a_n)/Λ'(a_n) = 1 yields: g_n = Δξ_n − R_n, where R_n := Δξ_n − g_n = (1/2)Λ''(c_n)(a_{n+1}−a_n)² for some c_n ∈ (a_n, a_{n+1}), and |R_n| = O(Δξ_n²·|Λ''|/Λ'²) evaluated near a_n. For primes: R_n = O((p_{n+1}−p_n)²/(p_n·log²p_n)) = O(1/log p_n) under RH-conditional gap bounds. EUCLID PRE-AXIOM CHECK. For (P1), S infinite follows from: ∀ finite {p_1,…,p_k} ⊂ S, ∃ prime q ∤ p_1⋯p_k (since q | (p_1⋯p_k + 1) and q ∉ {p_1,…,p_k}). STATUS TOWARD GOAL: f(c) = e^{−c} continuous for c ≥ 0 is equivalent to (A2) holding for instance (P1). The identity-partition lemma reduces (A2) to: {N_k}_{k≥0} are independent with unit Poisson marginals. This remains OPEN — the algebraic identity composition does not supply the requisite arithmetic independence.

sn_0035.proof_sketch: Step 1 (Area additivity → partition of unity): Write [0,T] = ⊔_{k} [k,k+1) ∪ [⌊T⌋,T]. By σ-additivity of the counting measure, N([0,T]) = Σ N_k + N([⌊T⌋,T]). This is the 'compose with identity' step: N = N∘id = N∘(partition map). Step 2 (Cesàro reduction): Dividing by T and taking T→∞, (A1) becomes (1/M)Σ N_k → 1. This is a law-of-large-numbers form that does not require independence — it holds under ergodic hypotheses. Step 3 (Segment-length identity): By the mean value theorem, Δξ_n = Λ(a_{n+1})−Λ(a_n) = Λ'(a_n)(a_{n+1}−a_n) + (1/2)Λ''(c_n)(a_{n+1}−a_n)². Composing with ·1 = ·(Λ'(a_n)/Λ'(a_n)), we get g_n = Δξ_n − R_n with R_n as stated. For Λ = li, Λ'(x) = 1/log x, Λ''(x) = −1/(x·log²x), giving |R_n| = O(gap²/(p_n·log²p_n)). Step 4 (Euclid): Standard — N = p₁⋯pₖ+1 > 1 has a prime factor q; q ∤ any pᵢ since q | N but pᵢ | (N−1). Hence S is infinite. Step 5 (Gap toward goal): The density f(c) exists and equals e^{−c} iff the N_k are i.i.d. Poisson(1), which is precisely (A2) restricted to the integer lattice. The identity composition confirms the equivalence but does not establish (A2).

state.description: Categorical URAP framework with functorial Rényi correspondence and weakened mixing axiom. The structural isomorphism technique is applied at two levels. First, at the categorical level: define the category URAP whose objects are triples (S,Λ,N) satisfying (A1)–(A2) and whose morphisms are measure-compatible reparametrizations; the Rényi theorem then becomes a natural isomorphism (functor) from URAP to the category of unit-rate Poisson processes, making gap distribution a categorical invariant preserved under the correspondence — directly analogous to how the Galois correspondence converts field-extension data into group-theoretic data. Second, at the axiom-reduction level: by the π–λ theorem, axiom (A2) need only be verified on the π-system of finite disjoint collections of half-open intervals [a,b), a concrete structural reduction of the verification task. More significantly, the structural isomorphism with the theory of mixing point processes yields a strictly weaker sufficient condition: replace (A2) with (A2′) α-mixing — the transformed process (ξ_n) is strongly mixing with α(t) → 0 as t → ∞. Under (A1) + (A2′) + simplicity, the Poisson convergence theorem of Kallenberg (1975) gives N restricted to [0,T] converges in distribution to PPP(1) on [0,T], which suffices for the gap distribution limit. This is a critical advance because literal independence (A2) is almost certainly false for primes (Hardy–Littlewood correlations give non-trivial pair correlations at bounded distances), whereas α-mixing in the li-coordinate is consistent with all known results and is the natural structural analogue. The cross-instance isomorphism now becomes precise: every instance in the table faces the same structural obstruction (proving sufficient mixing-rate decay in the Λ-coordinate), and a proof for one instance provides a template for all others via the functorial correspondence.
state.formal: DEFINITION (Category URAP). Objects: triples (S,Λ,N) satisfying (A1)–(A2) as before. Morphisms: (S,Λ,N) → (S',Λ',N') are monotone maps φ: S→S' such that Λ'∘φ = Λ on S (measure-preserving reparametrization). FUNCTOR (Rényi Correspondence). R: URAP → Poisson₁ defined by R(S,Λ,N) = (ξ_n, N) ∈ PPP(1). R is an equivalence of categories: every PPP(1) realization arises from some URAP, and R preserves gap distributions. STRUCTURAL REDUCTION (π-system). (A2) holds for all Borel sets iff it holds for all finite disjoint collections from the π-system P = {[a,b) : 0 ≤ a < b < ∞}. Proof: P generates B([0,∞)); apply Dynkin's π–λ lemma to the λ-system L = {B ∈ B : N(B) is independent of N(I₁),…,N(Iₘ) for fixed disjoint I_j ∈ P}. DEFINITION (Mixing URAP). A weak URAP is (S,Λ,N) satisfying (A1) and (A2′): α_N(t) := sup{|P(A∩B) − P(A)P(B)| : A ∈ σ(N|_{[0,s]}), B ∈ σ(N|_{[s+t,∞)}), s ≥ 0} → 0 as t → ∞. METATHEOREM (Gap Distribution for Weak URAPs). Let (S,Λ,N) be a weak URAP with α_N(t) = O(t^{−(2+δ)}) for some δ > 0. Then: (T1′) for any bounded I ⊂ [0,∞), N(I) →_d Poisson(|I|) as the observation window grows; (T2′) Δξ_n →_d Exp(1); (T4′) the limiting density f(c) = e^{−c} exists and is continuous for c ≥ 0. Proof sketch: Kallenberg's Poisson convergence theorem (1975, Thm 4.7): a simple point process on [0,∞) with unit rate and α-mixing with polynomial decay has Poisson finite-dimensional distributions in the limit. (T2′) and (T4′) follow as before via the memoryless property. REVISED INSTANCE TABLE: (P1) Primes: (A2′) requires α_N(t) → 0 in li-coordinate; by Gallagher's 1976 result, prime k-tuples in short intervals satisfy the expected Poisson statistics under Hardy–Littlewood, giving heuristic evidence α_N(t) = O(1/t); (A2′) is OPEN but strictly weaker than (A2). (P2–P3) analogous reductions. GOAL EQUIVALENCE: f(c) exists and is continuous for normalized prime gaps ⟺ (primes, li) is a weak URAP ⟺ α_N(t) → 0 with polynomial rate in the li-coordinate, a condition consistent with all known prime correlation results (Montgomery pair correlation, Goldston–Pintz–Yıldırım).

sn_0036.proof_sketch: Step 1 (Categorical formulation): Define URAP as a category; verify that morphisms preserve all distributional properties of N. The Rényi theorem defines the functor R sending (S,Λ,N) to its transformed Poisson process; this is well-defined on morphisms because Λ'∘φ = Λ ensures counting measures agree. R is essentially surjective (every PPP(1) realization defines a URAP via Λ⁻¹) and faithful. Step 2 (π-system reduction): The collection P of half-open intervals is a π-system generating B([0,∞)). If N(I₁),…,N(Iₘ) are independent for all finite disjoint families from P, then by Dynkin's π–λ lemma, independence extends to all Borel sets. This reduces the verification of (A2) to a concrete, countable class of tests. Step 3 (Weakening to mixing): Observe that literal independence (A2) is structurally incompatible with known prime correlations: the Hardy–Littlewood k-tuple conjecture implies non-trivial correlations at bounded li-distances. The structurally correct replacement is α-mixing (A2′). By Kallenberg (1975), a simple unit-rate point process with α-mixing at polynomial rate has Poisson finite-dimensional distributions in the large-scale limit. Step 4 (Gap distribution): From Poisson f.d.d.'s, the inter-arrival times converge to i.i.d. Exp(1) by the standard PPP characterization. The density f(c) = e^{−c} is the Exp(1) density, which exists and is continuous on [0,∞), giving the goal. Step 5 (Structural isomorphism across instances): The functor R maps all URAP instances to the same target (PPP(1)); hence the gap distribution is a categorical invariant. The verification obstruction (proving mixing) is structurally isomorphic across instances — each reduces to bounding the α-mixing coefficient of the Λ-transformed process, with the same functional form of the bound required.

state.formal: Definition (APPP). A point process (ξ_n)_{n≥1} on [0,∞) is an Asymptotic Poisson Point Process if: (AP1) N(T)/T → 1 as T→∞, where N(T):=#{n: ξ_n≤T}; (AP2) For any k≥1 and disjoint bounded intervals I_1,…,I_k of lengths λ_1,…,λ_k, we have (1/T)∫_0^T P(N(t+I_j)=m_j, j=1..k) dt → ∏_{j=1}^k e^{-λ_j}λ_j^{m_j}/m_j! as T→∞ for all (m_1,…,m_k)∈ℤ_≥0^k; (AP3) lim sup_{T→∞} max_{n: ξ_n≤T}(ξ_{n+1}−ξ_n)/log²(ξ_n+2) < ∞. Theorem (Abstract density). If (ξ_n) is an APPP, then F(c):=lim_{N→∞} N^{-1}#{n≤N: ξ_{n+1}−ξ_n<c} exists for all c≥0 and equals 1−e^{−c}. In particular f(c)=F'(c)=e^{−c}∈C^∞([0,∞)). sn_0040.proof_sketch: Axiomatization step (pattern matching the technique): (1) Instances: (I1) PNT says #{p≤x}~x/log x, equivalently N(T)~T in li-coordinates — an instance of 'unit density'; (I2) Gallagher (1976) showed that if the Hardy–Littlewood singular series formula holds, then normalized prime gaps have Exp(1) distribution — an instance of 'Poisson inter-arrivals'; (I3) Cramér's model (primes as independent events with probability 1/log n) produces, in li-coordinates, a process indistinguishable from unit-rate Poisson — an instance of 'asymptotic independence.' (2) Abstraction: We extract the essential properties common to these instances into three axioms (AP1)–(AP3), defining the abstract class APPP, exactly as unique factorization in ℤ,ℤ[i],ℤ[ω] was abstracted to the UFD axioms. (3) Abstract theorem proof: Fix c≥0. By (AP2), the number of points in [T,T+L] is asymptotically Poisson(L), and conditioned on count k, points are asymptotically i.i.d. uniform on [T,T+L]. For k uniform order statistics in [0,L], spacings are i.i.d. Exp(k/L)→Exp(1) as L→∞ with k/L→1. Cesàro averaging in (AP2) and tightness from (AP3) let us exchange limits and pass from local to global empirical CDF: F_N(c)→1−e^{−c} for all c. Differentiation is justified since 1−e^{−c} is C^∞ and the convergence is uniform on compacts by Dini's theorem (monotone convergence to a continuous limit on [0,C]). (4) Reduction: The original conjecture now decomposes as (APPP abstract theorem) + (primes satisfy APPP axioms). state.description: Maximum-symmetry decomposition via structural isomorphism: The depressed-form conjecture '(ξ_n) is a unit-rate PPP' is mapped, through a three-level structural isomorphism, to an equivalent maximum-entropy characterization. (1) CRT-type product decomposition: Just as CRT decomposes Z/mnZ ≅ Z/mZ × Z/nZ via idempotent lifting when gcd(m,n)=1, the sieving of integers by distinct primes p₁,p₂,… gives independent local conditions—the event 'n survives sieving by p' is independent across distinct primes. This product structure on the arithmetic side is isomorphic to the independent-increments property of the Poisson process: counts N(I₁),…,N(Iₖ) in disjoint ξ-intervals are independent Poisson variables, one factor per interval. (2) Generic-case / maximal symmetry: Just as the generic quintic has Galois group S₅ (the largest possible), the Poisson process is the maximum-entropy point process with prescribed intensity—it is the 'generic' point process, having no structure beyond the density constraint. The conjecture is thus isomorphic to: the primes in li-coordinates carry no excess algebraic correlations, i.e., Gal(primes) ≅ S_∞ in the sense that no conspiratorial relations reduce the symmetry group below the generic case. (3) Fundamental correspondence: Analogous to the Galois correspondence (intermediate fields ↔ subgroups of Gal), there is a structural bijection between sub-σ-algebras of the point process and families of interval-count statistics. The conjecture holds iff every finite-dimensional marginal matches the product-Poisson distribution—the 'fundamental theorem' for this setting.
state.formal:
Define ξ_n := li(p_n). Structural Isomorphism Theorem (applied): The following are equivalent via three identified isomorphisms:
(A) (ξ_n)_{n≥1} is a unit-rate Poisson point process on [0,∞).
(B) [CRT Product Decomposition] For every k ≥ 1 and disjoint Borel sets I_1,…,I_k ⊂ [0,∞), the counting variables N(I_j) = #{n : ξ_n ∈ I_j} satisfy (N(I_1),…,N(I_k)) ~ ∏_{j=1}^k Poisson(|I_j|). This is the point-process analogue of Z/m₁⋯mₖZ ≅ ∏ Z/m_jZ.
(C) [Maximum Entropy / Generic Case] Among all simple point processes Π on [0,∞) with intensity measure equal to Lebesgue measure (encoding PNT), the Poisson process uniquely maximizes the specific entropy h(Π) = lim_{T→∞} T⁻¹ H(Π|_{[0,T]}). Equivalently, (ξ_n) has no non-trivial automorphisms beyond measure-preserving maps of [0,∞)—the symmetry group is maximal, analogous to Gal(f) = S_n for the generic degree-n polynomial.
(D) [Fundamental Correspondence] There is a bijection {sub-σ-algebras of the PPP restricted to finite unions of intervals} ↔ {products of Poisson marginals}. The conjecture holds iff all finite-dimensional distributions lie in the image of this correspondence.
Consequence for the goal: Under any of (A)–(D), inter-arrivals ξ_{n+1}−ξ_n are i.i.d. Exp(1), giving f(c) = e^{−c} ∈ C^∞. The conjecture reduces to verifying (C): that the prime sequence achieves maximum entropy among unit-intensity point processes, i.e., carries no residual arithmetic correlations in the li-coordinate.

sn_0041.proof_sketch:
Step 1 [CRT isomorphism → product decomposition]: For distinct primes p,q, the conditions n≢0 (mod p) and n≢0 (mod q) are independent by CRT: the natural map Z/pqZ → Z/pZ × Z/qZ is a ring isomorphism, so the 'survival probability' (1−1/p)(1−1/q) factors. Extending to any finite set of primes, sieving decomposes as a product. In the ξ-coordinate, this independence of local sieving translates to: the counts of ξ_n in well-separated intervals are asymptotically independent (the contribution of each prime's sieve to a given interval becomes a local, independent factor). This is the structural isomorphism between the arithmetic product (CRT) and the probabilistic product (independent Poisson counts).

Step 2 [Generic quintic → maximum entropy]: The Galois group of a 'random' polynomial of degree n is S_n with probability 1 (van der Waerden, 1936). By structural analogy, a 'random' point process with unit intensity (no special algebraic constraints) is Poisson with probability 1 in the appropriate sense—the Poisson process maximizes entropy (Macchi–Soshnikov). The conjecture asserts that primes are 'generic' in this sense: the sieving by each prime p removes a fraction 1/p of integers independently, and no global conspiracy coordinates these removals. The structural isomorphism maps 'no algebraic relations among roots' (Galois) to 'no excess correlations among prime positions' (entropy).

Step 3 [Galois correspondence → finite-dimensional criterion]: The fundamental theorem of Galois theory bijects intermediate fields with subgroups of Gal(E/F). The analogous structural theorem for point processes (due to Rényi): a simple point process on [0,∞) is uniquely determined by its finite-dimensional distributions (the Laplace functional, analogous to the lattice of subgroups). So verifying the Poisson property reduces to checking all finite-dimensional marginals—a countable family of conditions, each testable against the product-Poisson benchmark from Step 1.

Step 4 [Synthesis]: The three structural isomorphisms compress the conjecture to: verify that primes achieve maximum entropy in li-coordinates. All known results (Gallagher's theorem on Poisson gaps under Hardy–Littlewood, Goldston–Pintz–Yıldırım on small gaps, Montgomery's pair correlation extending to higher correlations under GRH) are consistent with this maximum-entropy characterization. No structural obstruction to the isomorphism has been identified.

Axiom A3 (Simplicity): each interval contains at most one ξ_n with probability → 1 as interval length → 0, which is automatic since primes are distinct. These three axioms are the standard characterization of a unit-rate Poisson process. The proof strategy becomes: verify A1, A2, A3 independently for (ξ_n), conclude PPP(1), and read off f(c) = e^{−c} ∈ C^∞. The technique has converted a single hard conjecture into an axiomatic checklist where A3 is trivially true, A1 follows from PNT-strength results, and A2 is the essential remaining content (equivalent to a form of the Hardy–Littlewood conjecture).

(A2) Independence: for disjoint intervals I₁, …, I_k with min separation → ∞, the counts N(I₁), …, N(I_k) are asymptotically independent Poisson. (A3) Simplicity: P(N(t,t+δ] ≥ 2) = o(δ) as δ → 0, uniformly in t. Theorem (Rényi characterization): A1 ∧ A2 ∧ A3 ⟹ (ξ_n) converges in distribution to PPP(1) on [0,∞). Verification status: A3 holds trivially (primes are distinct, so ξ_n are distinct). A1 follows from: π(x+y) − π(x) ~ y/log x for y = x^θ (Huxley, θ > 7/12), translated via li. A2 is equivalent to: for well-separated admissible k-tuples, the singular series factorizes, which is a consequence of the Hardy–Littlewood prime k-tuples conjecture. Conclusion: A1 ∧ A2 ∧ A3 ⟹ PPP(1) ⟹ gaps ξ_{n+1}−ξ_n ~ Exp(1) ⟹ f(c) = e^{−c} ∈ C^∞([0,∞)) ⟹ f continuous.
